stances.claim: All candidates -- whether winners or losers -- must file with the Comelec their Statements of Contributions and Expenses (Soce) within 30 days from Election Day (by June 8, 2022) -- for four good-governance reasons: (1) check whether expenses were within statutory limits, (2) document specifically what expenses were for, (3) identify donors and their motives for large contributions, and (4) test whether donors and candidates could truly afford the alleged amounts.

RA 7166 Section 13's aggregate expense limits -- P10/registered voter for president and VP (about P675 million given the 67.5 million 2022 voters), P3 for senators and party-list reps, P5 for unaffiliated candidates -- have remained unchanged since 1991 even though campaign expenses may have 'ballooned 10 times,' so candidates report expenses 'much less than this limit -- to show faithful (even if sometimes incredible) compliance with the archaic law.'

OEC Section 102's enumerated permissible expense items create a tractable trackable-vs-untrackable asymmetry: candidates report mainstream-media ads (TV, radio, newspapers -- easily tracked) and 'simply ignore expenses that could not be easily tracked like cash given to local candidates and to their grassroots leaders, or for political rallies and contributions in kind.'

The law also requires donors and suppliers (under OEC Section 99) to file under-oath Soces with Comelec -- to enable double-checking candidate/party reports -- though 'many times, the large donors of the winners use their huge donations as badges to access government largesse.'
The Corporation Code, 'unknown to many,' bars ALL corporations from giving 'donations in aid of any political party or candidate or for purposes of partisan political activity.'

OEC Section 95 bars contributions from eight categories: (a) financial institutions; (b) public-utility/natural-resource operators; (c) government suppliers/contractors; (d) franchise/incentive/exemption holders; (e) borrowers of >P100,000; (f) educational institutions with public-fund grants; (g) Civil Service and AFP officials/employees; (h) foreigners.

While laudable, these transparency and accountability requirements have 'sadly become useless mountains of paperwork that have not reined in political expenses and corruption of voters.' The antiquated laws need to be revised: 'to keep up with the Internet Age,' to move backward the 90-day (national) and 45-day (local) reporting starting points to better capture year-ahead spending, and 'like in the United States, [to limit] contributions... to say P10,000 per donor to avoid huge political debts.'

notable_anecdotes: The 'faithful (even if sometimes incredible) compliance with the archaic law' aphorism -- capturing in a single phrase the disconnect between RA 7166's 1991 limits and 2022 campaign realities.
The 'badges to access government largesse' observation -- preserved as the column's most pointed structural-cynicism line about why large donors are not deterred by Soce disclosure.

Section 95's eight categories of prohibited contributors recited in full -- from financial institutions and public-utility operators down to foreigners -- modeling exhaustive-statutory-catalog discipline.

The 'useless mountains of paperwork' diagnosis paired with concrete reform proposals (Internet Age update; move 90-day/45-day windows backward; US-style ~P10,000 per-donor cap) -- the column's policy-prescription closing.

one_paragraph_summary: Why do all Philippine candidates -- winners and losers -- have to file with the Commission on Elections their Statements of Contributions and Expenses (Soce) within 30 days of Election Day (June 8, 2022 for the May 9 vote)? Panganiban's 'obvious IMHO' four-reason answer: for good governance, to find out whether expenses fell within statutory limits, what they specifically funded, who the donors were and their motives, and whether donors and candidates could truly afford the alleged amounts. RA 7166 Section 13 (passed 1991) sets aggregate expenditure limits at P10 per registered voter for president and VP (about P675 million given 67.5 million 2022 voters), P3 for senators and party-list reps, and P5 for candidates without party support. Three decades later, those limits remain unchanged though expenses 'may have ballooned 10 times,' producing 'faithful (even if sometimes incredible) compliance with the archaic law.' Beyond aggregate caps, OEC (BP Blg. 881) Section 102 itemizes the permissible expense categories -- travel, compensation of campaigners, telegraph/telephone tolls, stationery and printing, watchers, headquarters rent and maintenance, rallies, ads in mainstream media, counsel, voter-list copying, sample-ballot printing -- and creates a trackable-vs-untrackable asymmetry that candidates exploit: 'they simply ignore expenses that could not be easily tracked like cash given to local candidates and to their grassroots leaders, or for political rallies and contributions in kind.' Donors and suppliers (under OEC Section 99) must also file under-oath reports with Comelec -- designed to enable double-checking -- though 'many times, the large donors of the winners use their huge donations as badges to access government largesse.' The Corporation Code, 'unknown to many,' bars ALL corporations from political donations or partisan activity. OEC Section 95 then bars contributions from eight specific categories: (a) financial institutions, (b) public-utility/natural-resource operators, (c) government suppliers/contractors, (d) franchise/incentive holders, (e) borrowers of more than P100,000, (f) educational institutions with public-fund grants, (g) Civil Service and AFP officials/employees, and (h) foreigners. While 'laudable,' these transparency and accountability requirements have 'sadly become useless mountains of paperwork that have not reined in political expenses and corruption of voters.' CJ closes with reform proposals: revise the antiquated laws 'to keep up with the Internet Age,' move backward the 90-day (national) and 45-day (local) reporting windows to capture spending that begins 'a year or two ahead of Election Day,' and impose US-style per-donor caps of around P10,000 'to avoid huge political debts.'
